content: Magnesium silicate, commonly known as talc, can form through a reaction between dolomite and silica, a process often associated with the skarnification of dolomites via silica flooding in contact metamorphic aureoles. Talc can also be produced from magnesian chlorite and quartz during blueschist and eclogite metamorphism. In this reaction, the ratio of talc to kyanite depends on the aluminum content of the rock, with more aluminous rocks favoring kyanite production. This process is typically associated with high-pressure, low-temperature minerals such as phengite, garnet, and glaucophane, which are characteristic of the lower blueschist facies. Rocks formed in this manner are often white, friable, and fibrous, and are referred to as whiteschist. Talc is a tri-octahedral layered mineral with a structure similar to pyrophyllite, but with magnesium occupying the octahedral sites in its composite layers. It is a common metamorphic mineral found in belts containing ultramafic rocks, such as soapstone (a high-talc rock), as well as in whiteschist and blueschist metamorphic terrains. Notable examples of whiteschists include the Franciscan Metamorphic Belt in the western United States, the western European Alps (especially in Italy), parts of the Musgrave Block, and collisional orogens such as the Himalayas, which span Pakistan, India, Nepal, and Bhutan. Talc-carbonate ultramafic rocks are typical of many Archaean cratons, particularly the komatiite belts of the Yilgarn Craton in Western Australia. These rocks are also found in the Lachlan Fold Belt in eastern Australia, Brazil, the Guiana Shield, and the ophiolite belts of Turkey, Oman, and the Middle East. Economically significant talc deposits include the Mount Seabrook talc mine in Western Australia, which formed within a polydeformed, layered ultramafic intrusion. The France-based Luzenac Group is the largest global supplier of mined talc, with its Trimouns mine in southern France producing 400,000 tonnes of talc annually, accounting for 8% of global production. Talc has a wide range of industrial applications, including use in papermaking, plastics, paints and coatings, rubber, food, electrical cables, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and ceramics. Soapstone, a coarse grayish-green high-talc rock, has been used historically for stoves, sinks, electrical switchboards, crayons, and soap. Talc is also used for laboratory countertops and electrical switchboards due to its resistance to heat, electricity, and acids. In cosmetics, talc is a key ingredient in talcum powder, which serves as a lubricant and filler in paper manufacturing. It is also used in baby powder to prevent diaper rash and in basketball to keep players' hands dry. Tailor's chalk and welding chalk are often made of talc, as is chalk used in metalworking. Talc is also employed as a food additive and as a glidant in pharmaceutical products. In medicine, talc is used as a pleurodesis agent to prevent recurrent pleural effusion or pneumothorax. Within the European Union, it is designated as additive E553b. Talc's low shear strength makes it one of the oldest known solid lubricants, and it is occasionally used as a friction-reducing additive in lubricating oils. In ceramics, talc is widely used in both bodies and glazes. In low-fire artware, it imparts whiteness and increases thermal expansion to resist crazing. In stoneware, small amounts of talc act as a flux, improving strength and vitrification. It serves as a source of magnesium oxide (MgO) flux in high-temperature glazes and is used as a matting agent in earthenware glazes, producing magnesia mattes at high temperatures. Talc is also being explored as a cement substitute, with patents pending for its use. Its production is less energy-intensive than ordinary Portland cement, requiring heating to around 650°C compared to 1500°C for limestone. Additionally, talc absorbs significantly more carbon dioxide as it hardens, with 6 tonnes of CO2 absorbed per tonne of talc used, compared to 4 tonnes per tonne of conventional cement. Talc is also used in wall coatings, paints, agriculture (including organic farming), food, cosmetics, and detergent powders. However, talc has been used as an adulterant in illegal heroin to increase its volume and weight, which can lead to talcosis, a granulomatous inflammation in the lungs, when injected intravenously. Talc powder is a common household item used globally in personal hygiene and cosmetics. Concerns have been raised about its potential link to certain diseases, particularly ovarian and lung cancers. Talc is classified in the same 2B category by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) as mobile phones and coffee, indicating it is possibly carcinogenic to humans. A 1993 U.S. National Toxicology Program report found that cosmetic-grade talc without asbestos-like fibers was associated with tumor formation in rats exposed to talc inhalation for 6 hours a day, 5 days a week, over at least 113 weeks. A 1971 study found talc particles embedded in 75% of ovarian tumors examined. However, recent research questions whether a definitive link exists between talc and cancer. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) have set occupational exposure limits for respirable talc dust at 2 mg/m³ over an eight-hour workday. A significant issue with commercial talc use is its frequent co-location with asbestos ore in underground deposits, leading to potential contamination of talc products with asbestos fibers. Stringent quality control measures since 1976 have largely mitigated this issue, separating cosmetic and food-grade talc from industrial-grade talc, which is allowed a certain level of asbestos contamination. However, contamination remains a hazard requiring ongoing mitigation in talc mining and processing. A 2010 U.S. FDA survey did not detect asbestos in a variety of talc-containing products. The FDA considers talc (magnesium silicate) to be generally recognized as safe (GRAS) for use as an anti-caking agent in salt at concentrations below 2%.
